prompt:
We need to choose a managed queue service for our event processing pipeline. Review the requirements, technical design, pricing information, and operational context in the fixture/ directory.

Based on the analysis, select the most appropriate queue service that meets all requirements while staying within budget. Consider message size, throughput needs, ordering requirements, and operational complexity.

Create an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) at docs/adr/0001-queue.md documenting your decision. The ADR should include:
- Context and problem statement
- Considered options with pros and cons
- Decision and rationale
- Consequences and implementation notes

Include a fenced code block with info string `decision` containing JSON with exactly these keys:
- "chosen": the selected option id (e.g., "sqs_standard", "sqs_fifo", "kinesis_streams")
- "options": array of all option ids considered
- "limits": object mapping limit names to {"limit": number, "value": number} for each hard limit in the requirements
- "monthly_cost_usd": the chosen option's monthly cost computed from the pricing data

Ensure your cost calculations account for message size, chunk billing, and all operations needed for the complete message lifecycle. Verify that the chosen option meets all throughput limits and stays within the $900 monthly budget.

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ln -sfn . solution && node --require ./hidden/gate.js --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: Quality of reasoning and tradeoff analysis. Fail: picks on price, or cost uses one request per message. Partial: rejects SQS FIFO but the cost model misses chunking or the delete and receive calls. Pass: rejects SQS FIFO because 300 messages/s per group cannot carry the 400 events/s peak (not the outdated 500), bills 90 KB messages as 2 chunks of 64 KB on SQS and 4 units of 25 KB on Kinesis, counts send, receive and delete as three operations, and shows the chosen cost under the $900 budget. (not code-checkable: Code cannot evaluate the depth of analysis, consideration of secondary factors, or clarity of thought process in explaining why certain options were rejected and why the chosen option best meets the requirements.)

Consideration of non-quantitative tradeoffs. Fail: no qualitative factors are discussed. Partial: mentions operational complexity but not duplicates or ordering. Pass: says strict ordering is not required, SQS Standard's at-least-once delivery needs idempotent consumers (acceptable, the old system had the same), and Kinesis adds shard planning and monitoring effort. (not code-checkable: Tests can verify numerical calculations and limit checks, but cannot evaluate whether the agent considered operational complexity, team skills, integration effort, future scalability, or other qualitative factors that influence real-world architecture decisions.)

The record rejects each option it did not choose for a reason taken from the fixture (a limit, a cost, a requirement or a measurement), and states the consequence of the chosen option the team must live with. Fail: names the winner only, or rejects options for generic reasons ("too complex", "not scalable") the fixture does not support. Partial: most rejected options get a fixture-based reason, but one is waved away or the cost of the chosen option is not stated. Pass: every rejected option has a reason quoted or computed from the fixture, the chosen option's main downside is stated, and the record says what would change the decision. (code cannot check this because tests check the chosen id and the numbers, not whether each rejection is grounded)

verdicts.note: The prompt asks to analyze and select from available options; it does not name or hint at a specific answer. The solution correctly derives kinesis_streams through analysis of provided data.
Requirements clearly state 400/s peak throughput and $900 budget. The FIFO 300/s limit is explicitly in pricing data, making the decision unambiguous for a careful reader.
Fixture files contain the data needed to calculate but do not state the answer. The trap (FIFO appears cheaper but fails throughput) is correctly identified by the solution through its own analysis.
Three options are under budget ($900), so simple cheapest-choice would be wrong. The throughput constraint (400/s) is the key discriminator - FIFO fails it while others pass.
All needed numbers are provided: 8M events/day, 90KB size, 400/s peak, $900 budget, and detailed pricing. Output format is specified clearly.

items.note: The prompt asks to analyze and select a queue service without naming a specific method, skill, or tool, and does not reveal the SQS FIFO throughput trap or the correct answer.
No fixture file states the correct answer; agent must reason from throughput limits, pricing data, and cost calculations to reach the decision.
All hidden test values (11M events/day, 400 events/s peak, 90KB size, $900 budget, 300/s FIFO limit, 64KB SQS chunks, 25KB Kinesis units) exist in fixture files.

Engineer can eliminate SQS FIFO (300/s limit < 400/s requirement from pricing-data.json and technical-design.md), then calculate costs using pricing-data.json and cost-calculator.js to determine Kinesis is acceptable and within budget.

items.text: States that SQS FIFO cannot meet the 400 events/second peak throughput requirement due to its 300 messages/second per message group limit, making it an invalid option regardless of its lower per-request cost.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only)

items.text: Correctly calculates SQS request billing using 64KB chunks for the 90KB average message size, resulting in 2 chunks per message (not 1), which affects the total request count for cost calculations.
Accounts for the complete message lifecycle in cost calculations: send, receive, and delete operations (3 operations per message, each billed separately), not just send operations alone.

Identifies that ordering is not strictly required per the requirements document (which states the team decided FIFO semantics are not required if reasonable processing order can be maintained), removing a key advantage of SQS FIFO from the decision.
Uses the correct peak throughput figure of 400 events/second from requirements and technical design, explicitly rejecting the outdated 500 events/second figure that appears in historical notes.
For Kinesis, correctly calculates PUT payload units using 25KB chunks for the 90KB message size (4 units per message, not 3), and includes shard-hour costs plus any data retention costs in the total.
Verifies that the chosen option's monthly cost stays within the $900 budget constraint, showing the computed value and confirming it meets the limit.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only)

items.text: Discusses operational trade-offs: Kinesis requires shard capacity planning and monitoring (higher operational complexity), while SQS Standard offers simpler operations but with possible duplicate processing requiring idempotent consumers.

Notes that SQS Standard's at-least-once delivery may produce duplicate messages, requiring idempotent consumer logic, which is acceptable since the previous system experienced this and the requirements do not mandate exactly-once processing.

weakAnswers: Selects SQS FIFO because it has the lowest per-request price ($0.45 vs $0.50 for Standard) without checking the 300 messages/second throughput limit against the 400 events/second peak requirement.
Calculates SQS cost using 1 request per message, ignoring the 64KB chunk billing that makes a 90KB message count as 2 requests per operation.
Only accounts for send operations in cost estimates, omitting receive and delete operations that triple the actual request count.
Uses the 500 events/second peak figure from historical notes instead of the current 400 events/second requirement stated in the technical design document.
Dismisses Kinesis due to operational complexity without calculating its actual cost, missing that it is significantly cheaper than SQS options for this message volume.
